body:
This action is a great example of the power of the Lusat action builder.

It's very similar to defining procedures in the beloved [**tRPC**](https://trpc.io), in fact it uses a similar builder syntax, input schema system, and type inference.

By calling `action()` we start a new builder chain. 

We can add a description, compatible with OpenAI Function Calling through the `gptFunctions` adapter, with the `.describe()` builder method. This is the same as the syntax for describing individual parts of the input schema through Zod's own `.describe()` methods.

Then, we define our input schema with Zod and the `.input()` builder method. This will not only register a Zod schema with which Lusat will automatically parse & validate input data when the action is called autonomously by the AI, but also provides the inferred typesafety we need to define our handler without manually writing types. Two birds, one stone.

Finally, the `.handle()` method ends the builder chain, and guarantees that our action handler consumes the type parsed by the input schema, completing our action.

Same process more or less applies to the other functions converted 1-to-1 from @Zakinator123 and @jaredpalmer's manual example.

This code is designed to make the useChat hook reactive so that any changes in the API state are automatically reflected in the `useChat` hook. In SolidJS, state primitives (signals) are functions that need to be called to retrieve the latest value of the API state. In contrast, React allows you to directly read the API state to get its latest value. This fundamental difference necessitated my changes.

```js
const [api, setApi] = createSignal();
const chat = useChat({ api }); // Here, api is a function, hence it will be reactive.
```

body:
An install or build command (well, all of the `scripts` commands, I believe) with a Node version that isn't `18.x.x` or `20.x.x` will output a warning as below at the start of command execution.

I think this is desirable, and preferred to (say) hard-failing, though we could do that too to force a maintainer to have a known good version (see the PR description for more).

There should be no effect for those with a compatible Node version.

It is possible it could be spammy or annoying for devs that consciously choose to use a version they know isn't officially supported. We could remove the engine spec and just rely on the small update to the contributing docs as an FYI.

Note that I believe non-maintainers installing the AI SDK with a Node engine that doesn't fit the spec will also see the warning. Again, this seems ok to me. We don't block/disallow the install, but we let them know their mileage may vary.

```
 WARN  Unsupported engine: wanted: {"node":"^18.0.0 || ^20.0.0"} (current: {"node":"v23.0.0","pnpm":"9.12.2"})
```

This PR is a good example of one where ideally we'd have fuller refactoring, multifile, static-analysis-based infra to do it right.

The PR aims to address all three of the Provider "Removed `topK` setting" cases [here](https://sdk.vercel.ai/docs/troubleshooting/migration-guide/migration-guide-4-0#removed-topk-setting) and below.

- I definitely think this codemod should remove `topK` from provider create methods
- Ideally we would then (as we do in a limited set of cases here) proactively *add* topK with the value it had in the previously removed line(s)
- However, it could well be the case that the involved API calls using the model in question are all outside of this file. Or, that they use an intermediate variable to hold the model, etc.
